title: AI and bots on the campaign trail: What Poland can learn from Hungary
content:
On screen, a young Hungarian soldier stands on the Ukrainian front line. Moments later, he is killed, leaving a child crying at home. The scene looks like something from a war movie. But it was generated using artificial intelligence.

The video was published in February 2026 by the Budapest branch of Fidesz, Viktor Orbán’s party. Its message was clear: a victory for Péter Magyar’s opposition Tisza party could drag Hungary into war.

It was hardly an isolated incident. Ahead of the April 12, 2026, parliamentary election, artificial intelligence became one of the principal weapons in the political battle. Videos, images and other material were generated to attack opponents. They spread not only through official party accounts but also through affiliated organizations, influencers and networks of social media accounts.

“Using AI in political campaigns was not new. What was new during this election campaign was that they used it massively,” says Zsófia Fülöp, a journalist at the Hungarian fact-checking outlet Lakmusz who investigated disinformation during this year’s parliamentary election.

title: Helm from defence industry: The Omnibus is a luxury of peacetime
content:
The Czech defence industry exports approximately 90% of its production abroad. Couldn’t this high dependence on exports pose a risk in an environment of growing protectionism, should foreign markets stop purchasing our products?

Kristýna Helm: There will always be countries—and there are plenty of them—that lack certain technologies, won’t develop them, or would take an extremely long time to do so.

If I take one of our key markets—Indonesia—as an example, the defence industry there is more or less non-existent. And it is precisely these countries that seek out our technologies. Then there are countries like Denmark, where our company, Sellier & Bellot, supplies small-calibre ammunition. The Danes historically phased out ammunition production, and even though they are now trying to restart it, the process is taking a long time.

With certain technologies, it generally makes more sense to buy them rather than start manufacturing them. If we wanted to build fighter jets here in the Czech Republic, it would be much more expensive than buying them elsewhere.

content:

title: Estonia’s secret to a digital state: Trust, technology and less bureaucracy
content:
Karolina Zbytniewska, FocusEurope.pl: In Poland, responsibility for justice and digital affairs is divided between different government departments. The justice system deals with the judiciary, courts and judges. You are responsible for both justice and digital affairs. Why did Estonia decide to bring these areas together?

Liisa-Li Pakosta: We changed this model in 2024, although preparations had begun earlier, when the government started working on artificial intelligence initiatives.

We quickly realised that, since technology now makes practically everything possible, many of the challenges we face are primarily legal in nature.

At the same time, we had fully digitalised our judicial system. In practice, this means that many of the legal issues we deal with are directly connected to the digital sphere. Bringing these two areas together was therefore a natural decision.

title: Europe is not building a defensive fortress, but only national sandcastles
content:
Europe has awakened to a new security reality. One of the main topics of a recent online debate among politicians and experts from Czechia and Poland was the question of whether the European Union is allocating sufficient resources to its defence and whether it is able to invest them effectively.

According to Czech MEP Jan Farský (EPP), Europe’s fundamental problem is not a lack of funding or technological potential, but rather the deep fragmentation of national markets and military procurement.

“Europe is not weak. It’s just fragmented. We are losing our potential in national disputes. We still plan, purchase and produce largely along national lines and outside EU,” he emphasized.

Data illustrates the fragmentation of European armies. While the United States operates only 30 types of weapon systems on its territory, EU member states use approximately 178. This situation has led to major complications for Europe in logistics, maintenance, training, and the supply of spare parts.

title: There is now an alternative to Russian gas – but not yet to soaring prices
content:
According to GIE AGSI, the public gas storage platform for European gas infrastructure, Slovakia is currently receiving 486 GWh of gas per day, while withdrawals are approaching 615 GWh daily. With the heating season under way, an increasing share of these withdrawals is going directly to household consumption.

The energy content of the gas currently in storage stands at 20.5 TWh, representing 54.28% of Slovakia’s maximum gas storage capacity. This is below both Hungary’s storage level (77.5%) and the EU average (75%). Only Latvia has a lower figure in the statistics, at 50%.

At the same time, Slovakia’s storage capacity relative to its consumption is considerably higher than the EU average. Of the 3.5 billion cubic metres that can be stored, the majority – approximately 2.75 billion cubic metres – is held in NAFTA’s storage facilities near Láb, close to the Austrian and Hungarian borders.

These facilities are ideally positioned to receive and store both Russian gas arriving via TurkStream through Serbia and Hungary – at least for the time being – and gas delivered from Austria, including LNG unloaded at terminals in northern Germany.

title: “What Are They Not Telling Us?” Reminders to Prepare for Emergencies Fuel Anxiety About an Impending Crisis
content:
The posts claim that these announcements were made almost simultaneously and ask whether this means the whole world is preparing for war or another crisis. However, as Delfi’s investigation shows, some preparedness recommendations have been in place in many countries for years, while more recent information campaigns are linked to specific national civil protection and societal resilience plans, rather than an impending global catastrophe.

In October this year, posts began circulating on X, Threads and other social media platforms claiming that numerous countries around the world were, one after another, urging residents to prepare so-called 72-hour emergency bags or stocks of essential goods and supplies that would allow them to manage for at least three days without outside assistance. Reports that the US Department of Defense was planning to prepare military bases to operate for three months without external support added fuel to the fire.

These posts have reached very large audiences in a short time. For example, a post by an account called Whale News Daily on X has received more than 5.3 million views.

content:
Latvia’s Ministry of Defence (MoD) describes this narrative as part of the aggressor state’s information warfare, while military expert Mārtiņš Vērdiņš also says that, for now, it is a false alarm.

“Latvia currently faces no direct military threat,” says Ministry of Defence.

“Russia’s Defence Ministry is preparing to send reservists to territories along NATO countries’ borders, in what would be the largest deployment since the start of the so-called “special military operation”. Putin has approved the creation of a huge troop deployment corridor in north-western Russia. It is planned to stretch from Karelia to the Kaliningrad region. The backbone of this structure will consist of equipment storage bases, where newly manufactured tanks, armoured vehicles and artillery systems are already being delivered. The equipment is not yet being handed over to existing military units; instead, it is being stockpiled for units that will be formed after the reservists are deployed.

title: Former World Bank economist accuses Baltic States of irresponsibility but gets his facts wrong
content:
In one of them, the economist also links the Baltic States’ historical experience to the risk of the rest of the world facing a nuclear apocalypse. His original post garnered at least 621 000 views in just over a week.

“It is a strange world. Because three small Baltic countries have a population of 5.7 million (and a combined area smaller than that of some second-tier Chinese city), half of whom live in Europe, while another third are Russians who cannot obtain citizenship, and because they have trauma and bad memories of Soviet rule, the entire world of eight billion people is supposed to head towards a nuclear apocalypse and perish,” Branko Milanović wrote on X on the 19th of October.

After the post was published, people from the Baltic States pointed out factual inaccuracies, including questioning the population and ethnic composition figures he cited. Commenters also said that Milanović’s remarks echoed Kremlin propaganda narratives.

In response to the criticism, Milanović published another post on 22 October, clarifying that his original post had referred to ethnic Russians rather than non-citizens.
